INTRODUCTION
As humanity begins to expand into & beyond low-Earth orbit for sustained
periods, developing a new set of strategies is paramount to the success of our
habitation in these extreme environments. Among those integral elements,
growing fresh produce with astro-agriculture, and cultivating & processing
biological organisms, is paramount in providing nutrition for extended-duration
missions, psychological well-being (Zhang et al, 2020) & resource efficiencies.
Unsurprisingly, the gravity anomalies experienced in off-world habitats
substantially affect plant development, rendering traditional agronomy obsolete.
The opportunity to leverage the beneficial effects of gravity on biological
organisms’ growth presents an under-utilized opportunity to support more hardy,
consistent production. Accordingly, pioneering strategies centered around plant
adaptation to zero-or-partial gravity situations emerge as crucial to our pursuit of
life amongst these cosmic frontiers and critical to address our need for renewable
sources of sustenance, on and off-world.
Background
In plants grown on Earth’s surface, geotropism and gravitropism are virtually
synonymous, however, in space (and in this experiment) it is vital to note the subtle
distinction between the two. Gravitropism is a special case of geotropism; It
possesses its own implied vector metric: positive gravitropism is when a plant
grows towards the source of gravity (activated by the amyloplast in the roots) while
negative gravitropism is when a plant grows away from the source of gravity
(Lopez, et al., 2014). All gravitropic movements can be considered geotropic, but
not all geotropic movements involve gravity detection and induce a response
specific to plants.
3

-The GeoGro Team
-
The basic principles governing gravitropism, particularly the consistent downward
growth of plant roots, are believed to rely on the Cholodny-Went hypothesis. This
concept suggests that the perception of gravity induces lateral redistribution of the
phytohormone, auxin, within the plant, thereby triggering differential growth
between the lower & upper sides of the affected organ, which leads to directed
curvature towards the source of gravity. Thus, the Cholodny-Went model forms
the foundation for our comprehension of Gravitropism in plants (Cholodny, 1927;
Went, 1928; Orbovik and Poff, 1993; Sato et al, 2014).
Auxins are a class of phytohormones that have a pivotal role in coordinating
various aspects of plant growth and development. Specifically, auxins play a direct
and critical role in ensuring the proper coupling of cell growth and proliferation
under normal terrestrial conditions. Auxins mediate the link between detected
stimuli and subsequent cellular responses in plants. By functioning as signaling
molecules, auxins enable cells to detect and react appropriately to environmental
cues, thereby facilitating the activation of downstream molecular events that
ultimately shape plant growth and behavior. Through careful modulation of auxin
production, distribution, and breakdown, plants dynamically adjust their
physiological activities to match prevailing circumstances best (Muday and
Murphy, 2002; Medina and Herranz, 2010).
Furthermore, auxins exert a major influence on the decoupling of these processes
under altered gravity conditions, such as during spaceflight. At the cellular level,
auxins primarily regulate meristematic competence, which encompasses the
capacity to coordinate cell growth and proliferation in distinct zones within plant
roots. (Bhalerao and Bennet, 2003; Taele et al, 2006). These zones correspond to
regions where cell division, expansion, and differentiation occur, allowing for the
maintenance of appropriate cell number and size (Perrot-Rechenmann, 2010).
It is widely understood that plant organs have a growth orientation in response to
gravity. The input (gravity sensing) in cells and then signal conversion (gravity
signaling) progress sequentially which then in turn triggers the next step which
redirects auxin transport toward the lower flank of the plant organ (Nakamura,
4

-The GeoGro Team
-
2019). When gravity alteration takes place, a change is produced within the lateral
balance of the auxin signaling process, resulting in the loss of orientation,
ultimately altering the gravitropism of the plant (Gadella, 2018).
Notably, the disturbance of gravity during spaceflight triggers a notable stress
reaction in plants, likely attributable to the loss of meristematic competence,
underscoring the importance of auxins in mediating plant responses to changing
environmental conditions (Medina, 2021). The close association between cell
growth & proliferation constitutes a hallmark feature of meristematic cells,
rendering the dissociation of these two cellular processes triggered by microgravity
conditions. It is helpful to remember that this is a significant source of stress for
these specialized cells. Typically, tight synchronization of cell growth and
proliferation ensures optimal plant development, tissue regeneration, and response
to environmental perturbations.
Nevertheless, under microgravity conditions, such strict coordination becomes
compromised, potentially giving rise to deleterious consequences, notably the
undue accumulation of damaged cells, diminished photosynthetic efficiency, and
hampered biomass accretion. This is seen in multiple studies that observe an
increase in cell proliferation but a decrease in cell growth in space. Past studies
suspect that these observed results were due to alterations in the regulation of the
cell cycles. (González-Camacho et al, 2021; Manzana et al, 2018; Matia et al, 2010).
Additional studies imply that modified gravity impacts cell growth and
proliferation via the transduction of the gravitropic signal initially received by
columella cells located within the root tip. Specifically, alterations in gravity
translate to altered cell division and expansion through the actions of these
specialized gravity sensor cells (Medina and Herranz, 2010).
Hence, identifying effective countermeasures against microgravity-induced
uncoupling assumes paramount importance in advancing our understanding of
plant adaptation and resilience in extreme habitat settings, eventually contributing
to the design of functional bio-regenerative life support systems required for
5

-The GeoGro Team
-
extended stays in environmental scenarios like those found on the Moon, Mars,
and other extraterrestrial environments.

Enclosure

variable data was increased. The apparatus
was constructed of an outer 9U server rack
with a pull-out equipment tray installed on the lowest rung. A peristaltic pump to
dispense timed & dosed water into the experiment was affixed to the far left corner
of the container alongside a water collection tray at the very bottom. A gold radiant
barrier, which was used as a light reflector, was hung on 3 sides of the container
and the top as well.
A full spectrum LED Grow Light with 144
LEDs (74 Cold
White + 46 Warm White + 20 Red + 2 Purple + 2 Dark Red) was hung from above 8
inches from the surface of where the plants were grown. Upon the equipment tray
there were multiple hardware components mounted. Before anything else could be
affixed, first, supports for the motors and
tensioners were attached to the tray. Next,
an
embedded
system
running
a
linux
server was attached and connected to three
NEMA motors(two for the drive system
and one for the peristaltic pump). Also
connected
were
2
Arduino
microcontrollers, one for the drive system
6

-The GeoGro Team
-
and one for the lights & water pump. A stepper driver hat was used to run the drive
system. Additionally connected was a light meter, a hygrometer, dew points sensor.
Next, both were wired and programmed control modules to collect and record data
continuously and maintain prescribed rotational drive parameters. Belts were
affixed to two of the three-cylinder apparatuses & these were programmed to
rotate at the predetermined rates, as laid forth in our hypothesis (2 rpms & 4 rpms).
As the control cylinder would have no reason to rotate, there was no belt connected
as it remained stationary throughout the experiment. This is all held aloft by two
A-frame mounts on either side of the equipment tray.
Water Core
To provide hydration to the specimens, the design called for a central pipe to carry
water through the center of each cylinder, a water core. A 17mm(outside diameter)
pipe was used for this purpose and also acted as a central axel for the cylinders to
freely rotate around. This pipe was machined with 18 total - six 2mm equidistant
holes for each of the three-cylinder segments using a laser beam and a drill press.
The capillary cloth was then around the water core to prevent soil from plugging
up the irrigation holes and facilitate even distribution of water around the soil
mass. Connecting to one side of the watercore/pipe was a tube running from the
peristaltic pump, which delivered 1-deciliter of 6-stage reverse osmosis filtered
water on a 12-hour timer to deliver from a water reservoir. (We did not use a
bladder as planned due to pressure & siphon effects.)
Cylinders
Rather than traditional pots, our experiment called for the design and fabrication
of three hollow cylinders. These cylinders would be filled with the lunar simulant /
soil mixture and act as the receptacle for the plants to germinate & grow. End caps
were affixed to either side of the cylinder to give it structure; the cylinders
consisted of a single surface membrane and two end caps; and made entirely of
HDPE. (See figures 1,2) This material was used as other plastics tend to leach
chemicals into soil and wanted to avoid that. Both 1/16th inch surface members &
7

1/2 inch end caps were designed in CAD and cut with a CNC router. Having been
drilled intact everything was assembled with machine screws. Both sides end caps
were equipped with bearings (as seen in figures 3,4,5) that allows the cylinders to
freely revolve around the fixed water core as a central fixed axle.
Figure 1: Design of the cylinder panels
Figure 2: Cylinder cutouts ready for assembly
Using CAD/CAM software and CNC hardware, we were able to ensure design
fidelity and dimensional accuracy while minimizing any margin for error.
Figure 3 4,5 : Cylinder fabrication overview
Timing belts attached to each cylinder's end caps and independent stepper motors
provided reliable, and accurately controlled rotations per unit.

Rooting Baskets & Burlap Encasement
In order to prevent the soil from falling out we used a
combination of burlap and 3D printed ‘rooting baskets’.
The design called for a small cage to hold a seed in
before being thrust through the burlap into the soil
mass; it would mechanically interface and lock into the
cylinder for stability. The design went through to
different versions. The initial one worked well, meeting
minimum requirements; however, did not fit entirely
flush to the cylinder; it was redesigned to allow for
greater retention within the grow port interface.
The second version increased surface area interface for
mechanical connection and fit flush. You can see this in
the below diagrams and the Appendix.
See Photos in the Appendix for more Diagrams
of our experimental apparatus
EXPERIMENT
Experiment Abstract
The experiment displays the effects of two(2) different rates of geotropism on
plants, here, on earth by propagating them in a mix of soil, and the provided
Lunar-regolith-like simulant. The experiment consists of three(3) hollow
horizontal cylinders: one stationary cylindric control group, one slowly rotating
cylinder, and one more rapidly rotating cylinder. All cylinders were held aloft by
supporting ‘racks’ and will be filled with a 50% Lunar-regolith simulant, and 50%
soil blend. Cavities were bored into these cylinders, ‘grow-ports’, and ‘rooting
baskets’ were 3D printed & seeds were sown, with the intention for plants to grow
outwards orthogonal to their cylinders’ axis of rotation. Each cylinder housed and
grew three Arugula, three Red Romaine, and three WheatGrass specimens.

Fresh Weight
On March 14th, 2024, 31 days after the start of the experiment, we used a knife to
cut and separate our three samples from the cylinder in order to get a
measurement of their fresh weight.
We measured a .01 gram digital scale with the weight of a small plastic bag and
then proceeded to take the measurement of biomass. See figures below.
RPM 0 : 5.53 grams
RPM 2 : 5.14 grams
RPM 4 : 1.30 grams
Vitamin C
The biomass of each sample was then removed from the bags and subsequently
ground to a pulp the biomass to utilize vitamin C strips to measure Vitamin C
levels. We exposed the reagent on the vitamin C test strips for 2 seconds to get the
measurement and then waited 30 seconds for the reagent to react and then visually
compared the color to a table to ascertain the vitamin C levels present in the
samples.

DISCUSSION & CONCLUSIONS
Our study set out to examine whether prolonged exposure to rotational stimuli
during the growth cycles of select species would confer a favorable adaptive
response mechanism within their morphology. Preliminary visual inspections
displayed encouraging signs consistent with positive responses, such as improved
morphologic appearance up till a particular juncture. Surprisingly, contrary to our
working hypothesis, the obtained results yielded an exact reverse trend once
measurements were compiled at the conclusion of the study.
We suspect and substantiate our suspicions with photographic records that the
total mass produced by the specimen rotating at 4 rpm surpassed the load and
space limits tolerated by our prototype apparatus. Throughout consecutive stages
of the trial period, we show in the figures provided, that the specimen begins to
exhibit signs of stress. Photographic records show the specimen being subjected to
mechanical stress forces such as colliding with the inner wall and floor of the
apparatus due it’s increase in size compared to the other two test groups. This
inevitably skewed the intended outcomes unfavorably.
This is seen in past studies showing that the challenges with long term experiments
conducted with rotational machines have challenges relating to the increased mass
of the plant specimens, the changing weight distribution, the bending stress and
other random mechanical stimulation it ultimately causes. (van Loon et al, 2007;
Manzano et al., 2009)
While the ultimate outcome of our study did not align with our initial hypothesis,
the earlier weeks of our specimen’s growth did. The initial vegetative growth of the
specimen rotating at 4 rpm indicates an acceleration within germination occuring
up until the point of mechanical interference.
In addition to our obstacles with the mechanical stress force, there were also
challenges with our light intensity causing the red roman and arugula to seemingly
sprout but not grow past the germination phase. We also had issues with our
16

-The GeoGro Team
-
hygrometer exporting and deleting date, this break of data can be seen in the above
results section.
Due to the promising growth in the initial stages, we still theorize that if these
challenges are circumvented the implication is large for the practical application
involving rotational spin and sustainable plant growth within outer space. It is
suspected that the rotational spin altered the mesomatic competence of the plant
affecting the auxins signaling.
Further studies should also examine the following unresolved questions.
●
How do alterations in varied gravitational stimuli impact fundamental plant
growth metrics?
●
How does rotational stimuli affect the auxin mesomatic competence of the
plant?
●
Does a spinning rotational machine provide a significant enough
improvement in plant growth to warrant such an apparatus?
●
What implications does this discovery hold for improving future
explorations in astro-agriculture & terrestrial crops, alike?
●
How does rotational stimuli affect the auxin mesomatic competence of the
plant?
To effectively build upon prior learnings and render significant strides towards
progressive achievements, we recommend the following experimental
improvements -
●
Optimize hardware configurations accommodating wider spectra of plant
dimensions to prevent premature failures linked to excess bulk burden.
●
Employ cutting-edge imaging modalities for extracting detailed metric
intelligence tracking incremental adjustments occurring within plant tissue
layers.
●
Develop comparative analytics
17

-The GeoGro Team
-
●
Explore and find the diminishing point of return on cylinder rotation speed
for various genotypes and phenotypes.
●
Alternating and exploring light frequencies and intensities.
Currently there’s limited studies that explore the direct relationship between plant
rotation and auxin concentration fluctuations. Nonetheless, indirect evidence
suggests that rotation induces mechanical forces that are beneficial for the growth
of plants in potential space environments. This phenomenon exhibits promising
implications for tailored optimization of rotation strategies promoting improved
plant health and stability within spacecraft ecosystems.
